newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Ung Huot says king approves government.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Ung Huot says king approves government.

text.p: Cambodia's newly appointed First Prime Minister Ung Huot said on Thursday that King Norodom Sihanouk had given his blessing to Phnom Penh's new government during a meeting in Beijing.
Ung Huot and his powerful co-premier, Hun Sen, had five hours of talks with Sihanouk at the king's Beijing residence on Tuesday.

"The king gave us his blessing and recognises the prime minister," Ung Huot told reporters at Phnom Penh airport upon his return from Beijing, where Sihanouk has been receiving medical treatment since February.
Hun Sen toppled Sihanouk's son, Prince Norodom Ranariddh, on July 6 and then backed Ung Huot's nomination to replace the ousted prince.
He had previously ruled with Ranariddh in an uneasy coalition government that took power after U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993.
Last week Sihanouk called Ung Huot a "puppet" of Hun Sen and said he still recognised Ranariddh as the legitimate first premier.

Ung Huot showed reporters a copy of a news agency report that had been annotated by Sihanouk. Next to a section of the report that said the Cambodian delegation had come to seek the king's blessing, the monarch had written: "At lunch, I toasted their health."
"That means the king already gives his blessing," Ung Huot said, pointing to Sihanouk's hand-written note.
Political analysts in Phnom Penh said the king's approval was the last hurdle facing Hun Sen in his bid to legitimise his new government.
Sihanouk had offered to abdicate on Monday, but said later that in their Tuesday meeting, Hun Sen had refused the offer.

The king said on Thursday he would return to Cambodia before the end of the month to hold a Buddhist ceremony for peace and national reconciliation in Siem Reap, home of the famed Angkor temple complex.
Hun Sen told reporters he had assured Sihanouk that he was the defender of the monarchy.
"There were some people who reported to him that I will completely destroy the monarchy," Hun Sen told reporters.
"I told the king and queen, please consider us the defenders of the monarchy. If anyone wants to end the monarchy, they have to put an end to my life first," he said.

Hun Sen said the king also would attend the first meeting of Cambodia's Supreme Council of Magistry, a body, yet to be set up, that will oversee the functioning of the judicial system. But he gave no date.

Hun Sen also dismissed a suggestion from the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) that an informal meeting of all parties involved in the Cambodian problem be held, including Ranariddh and Hun Sen.
"Any attempt to call an informal meeting between the government of Phnom Penh and Ranariddh would be a waste of time," Hun Sen said.
ASEAN postponed Cambodia's entry to the group after Ranariddh was overthrown and has been trying to mediate a solution to the country's problems.
Hun Sen insisted that if Ranariddh returns to Cambodia, he would have to face charges for illegal negotiations with the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group and for alleged weapons smuggling.
Last week the Cambodian National Assembly voted to strip Ranariddh of his parliamentary immunity and a military court subsequently issued a warrant for his arrest.
Asked if Ranariddh would be allowed to take part in an election planned for May next year, Hun Sen said: "The question of joining the election or not, you have to ask the court."
